Everything up to this post has been me writing the pipeline logic myself: call
this tool, then that one. Planning flips that around, an LLM looks at a task
and produces the plan itself, which I then execute. And once a task needs
genuinely different kinds of expertise, I stop trying to make one agent do
everything and split it into a team instead, the same instinct that led me to
split my own error-analysis and ingestion agents apart rather than bolt
everything onto one.

## Jargon, explained simply

**Planning.** An LLM deciding the sequence of steps needed to complete a task,
instead of a developer hard-coding that sequence.

**JSON plan.** A plan expressed as a structured list of steps, which your code
then reads and executes one by one.

**Code-as-plan.** A plan expressed as actual runnable code the model writes,
more flexible, riskier to run unsupervised.

**Linear pattern.** A fixed sequence of agents, each one's output feeding
directly into the next, with no agent deciding what happens next.

**All-to-all pattern.** Every agent can message any other agent freely, and the
group is done once one agent declares the task complete.

**Orchestrator.** Whatever decides the order agents run in, either your own
code, in the linear pattern, or the agents themselves, in the all-to-all
pattern.

## Planning: letting the model decide the steps

A JSON plan is a structured list of steps the model outputs, which your code
then walks through and executes. A code-as-plan approach has the model write
actual Python that does the work, which you then run directly.

```python
import aisuite as ai
import json

client = ai.Client()

response = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="openai:gpt-4o-mini",
    messages=[
        {"role": "system", "content": "You are a segmentation pipeline planner. "
         "Respond only with a JSON list of steps, each with a tool name and arguments."},
        {"role": "user", "content": "New X-ray scan just came in as scan_0602.tif. "
         "Plan how to process it end to end, from raw file to a void-ratio verdict."}
    ]
)

plan = json.loads(response.choices[0].message.content)
for step in plan:
    print(step["tool"], step["arguments"])
```

The tradeoff is real, and I feel it every time I consider using this in
production: a fixed pipeline I write by hand is predictable and easy to debug.
A model-generated plan can adapt to unusual cases, an unusually noisy scan
might get an extra denoising step the model decides to add on its own, but it's
harder to guarantee what it will do on any given run. I lean toward fixed
pipelines for anything that ends up in a report, and reserve model-generated
plans for exploratory work.

## Multi-agent systems: specialists instead of one generalist

Once a task needs genuinely different expertise, preprocessing logic, model
inference, postprocessing rules, error triage, it works better as a team of
small, focused agents than one agent trying to do everything. The course walks
through communication patterns in increasing order of complexity and
decreasing order of predictability. I'll build the two ends of that spectrum:
linear and all-to-all.

## Pattern one: the linear pipeline

The simplest and most predictable pattern, a fixed sequence, each agent's
output feeding directly into the next, no agent deciding what happens next, my
Python function is the orchestrator. This mirrors the course's own four-agent
marketing lab, just rebuilt for segmentation.

```python
import aisuite as ai

client = ai.Client()

def preprocessing_agent(raw_path):
    return normalize_xray(raw_path)

def modeling_agent(normalized_path):
    return {"mask_path": normalized_path.replace(".png", "_mask.png")}

def postprocessing_agent(mask_path):
    return check_void_ratio(mask_path)

def error_analysis_agent(verdict_text):
    response = client.chat.completions.create(
        model="openai:gpt-4o-mini",
        messages=[
            {"role": "system", "content": "You are an error-analysis agent for a "
             "semiconductor imaging pipeline."},
            {"role": "user", "content": "Given this verdict, decide if it needs "
             "human review and why: " + verdict_text}
        ]
    )
    return response.choices[0].message.content

def run_segmentation_pipeline(raw_path):
    normalized = preprocessing_agent(raw_path)
    model_output = modeling_agent(normalized)
    verdict = postprocessing_agent(model_output["mask_path"])
    review_decision = error_analysis_agent(verdict)
    return review_decision

print(run_segmentation_pipeline("scan_0602.tif"))
```

Four specialists, one fixed order, easy to trace, easy to debug. This is
basically the shape my own ingestion and error-analysis agent split already
takes, just with two more stages spelled out explicitly here.

## Pattern two: all-to-all

At the other extreme, every agent can message every other agent whenever it
wants, each is prompted with knowledge that the others exist, and the group
converges when one agent self-declares the work complete. The course is
explicit that this suits applications where some unpredictability is
tolerable, not production systems, you simply re-run it if the output is not
good enough.

```python
class Agent:
    def __init__(self, name, role_prompt, client):
        self.name = name
        self.role_prompt = role_prompt
        self.client = client
        self.inbox = []

    def receive(self, sender, message):
        self.inbox.append({"from": sender, "message": message})

    def act(self, other_agent_names):
        context = "\\n".join(f"{m['from']}: {m['message']}" for m in self.inbox)
        prompt = (
            self.role_prompt + "\\n\\nOther agents in this team: " +
            ", ".join(other_agent_names) +
            "\\n\\nConversation so far:\\n" + context +
            "\\n\\nRespond with either a message to a specific agent in the "
            "format TO:<agent_name> <message>, or DONE: <final summary> if the "
            "team's task is complete."
        )
        response = self.client.chat.completions.create(
            model="openai:gpt-4o-mini",
            messages=[{"role": "user", "content": prompt}]
        )
        return response.choices[0].message.content


def run_all_to_all(agents, max_rounds=6):
    for round_num in range(max_rounds):
        for agent in agents.values():
            other_names = [n for n in agents if n != agent.name]
            reply = agent.act(other_names)

            if reply.startswith("DONE:"):
                return reply

            if reply.startswith("TO:"):
                target_name, _, message = reply.partition(" ")
                target_name = target_name.replace("TO:", "").strip()
                if target_name in agents:
                    agents[target_name].receive(agent.name, message)
    return "No agent declared completion within max_rounds."


agents = {
    "preprocessing": Agent("preprocessing",
        "You handle normalization of raw X-ray TIFFs.", client),
    "modeling": Agent("modeling",
        "You run the segmentation model and report mask statistics.", client),
    "error_analysis": Agent("error_analysis",
        "You review results from other agents and flag anything implausible, "
        "declaring DONE once you are satisfied the case is resolved.", client),
}

print(run_all_to_all(agents))
```

I have noticeably less control here than in the linear version. No agent is
guaranteed to talk to any other in a given order, and the whole thing could, in
principle, loop past max_rounds without resolving, which is exactly why the
course frames this as chaos-tolerant, and why I cap it with max_rounds at all.

## Which pattern for which job

For anything going into a production KPI report, a regulated defect log, or
anything I need to explain to an auditor, I use the linear pattern, or the
hierarchical manager pattern one step up, single point of control, easy to
reason about. I reach for all-to-all only for exploratory, low-stakes work,
brainstorming a new synthetic-data augmentation strategy, for example, where
some unpredictability is genuinely fine.
